title: What is the shortest toran both strip makers can make?
description: Two toran makers use strips of six and eight centimetres, and each list of possible lengths is written out. The lengths found in both lists are called common multiples, and the smallest one is the shortest toran both can make. Keeko doubts this and wants six times eight, which is not the shortest.
teaching_notes: One idea: list the multiples of each strip length and look for the first length found in both lists. Watch for students who multiply the two strip lengths and take that as the shortest, when a smaller common length hides in the lists.

source: {{NAME_3}} uses strips of 6 cm and {{NAME_4}} uses strips of 8 cm. List the toran lengths each can make, and find the lengths both can make.
video_script.why: The child knows multiples from earlier classes and needs to see that a toran made of whole strips has a length that is a multiple of the strip length.
video_script.substitution: Write the multiples of each strip length, pick the lengths found in both lists, and take the smallest as the shortest toran.
video_script.anchor: Two rows of cloth strips, 6 cm strips in one row and 8 cm strips in the other, placed one next to another to make torans, with length labels below.
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko takes the shortest toran as six times eight, which is forty eight centimetres. Forty eight works, but twenty four is in both lists and comes first.
video_script.payoff_line: The shortest toran both can make is twenty four centimetres

names.{{NAME_3}}: makes torans with 6 cm strips of cloth
names.{{NAME_4}}: makes torans with 8 cm strips of cloth

never_show: 48 cm as the shortest toran, marked right
maths_rules: {{NAME_3}} can make 6, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36, 42, 48 cm, the multiples of 6
{{NAME_4}} can make 8, 16, 24, 32, 40, 48, 56 cm, the multiples of 8
lengths in both lists: 24 and 48 cm, the common multiples of 6 and 8
the smallest is 24 cm, so the shortest toran is 24 cm
slip: 6 × 8 = 48 cm works, 48 = 8 × 6 = 6 × 8, but 24 = 4 × 6 = 3 × 8 comes first
video_script.design: One idea: a toran of whole strips has a length that is a multiple of the strip length, and the shortest toran for both is the first length in both lists. The two lists stay on the board from step one to the answer.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>This is a question from your book.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>{{NAME_3}} makes torans from strips of cloth, six centimetres long.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>{{NAME_4}} makes torans from strips that are eight centimetres long. Strips are placed one next to another.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>Both want torans of the same length. What is the shortest toran they can both make?

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

marks.m1: one 6 cm strip is shown and copies are added one after the other
marks.m2: the lengths 6, 12 and 18 are labelled multiples of 6
marks.m3: a length found in both strip rows is boxed and labelled common multiple

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>A toran is made of whole strips, so its length grows by one strip at a time.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Each such length is called a multiple of the strip length.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>A length that is a multiple of both strip lengths is called a common multiple.

marks.m1: the given line is written in the working band

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>We have to find the lengths both can make, and the shortest one.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>The shortest toran both can make is twenty four centimetres.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>It takes four strips of six, or three strips of eight.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Keeko thinks the shortest toran is six times eight.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>That is forty eight centimetres, and forty eight does work.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>But twenty four is also in both lists, and it comes first.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>Multiplying the two lengths gives a common multiple, but not always the lowest one. We look through the lists for the first match.
